07-Security/15-API-Groups:
### Introduction

All Kubernetes capabilities are exposed through the REST API, organised into groups. Understanding groups is needed for RBAC rules (`apiGroups`).

### Two categories

| Category | Path | Resources |
|---|---|---|
| Core (legacy) | `/api/v1` | pods, namespaces, nodes, services, configmaps, secrets, PV, PVC, events |
| Named | `/apis/<group>/<version>` | apps, batch, networking.k8s.io, rbac.authorization.k8s.io, storage.k8s.io, certificates.k8s.io, policy, autoscaling |

```
/api/v1/pods
/apis/apps/v1/deployments
/apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/networkpolicies
/apis/certificates.k8s.io/v1/certificatesigningrequests
```

Within each group are **resources** and **verbs** (`list, get, create, delete, update, patch, watch`).

### Discovering

```bash
kubectl api-resources -o wide              # kind, group, namespaced, verbs
kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps
kubectl api-versions
curl http://localhost:8001/apis | grep name
kubectl proxy 8001 &
```

### Versions

`v1` (stable), `v1beta1` (beta, may change), `v1alpha1` (alpha, disabled by default). Preferred version is chosen by the API Server.

### Why it matters

An RBAC rule must name the right group:

```yaml
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]           # core group is the empty string
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get","list"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["create"]
```

### Key takeaways

- Core group is `""`; others have names; check with `kubectl api-resources`.
07-Security/16-Authorization:
### Introduction

Once authenticated, the API Server must decide whether the identity can perform an action. Authorization restricts users to the minimum permissions they need.

### Mechanisms

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| **Node** | Authorises kubelets (identities `system:node:<name>` in group `system:nodes`) to read what their Pods need |
| **ABAC** | Policy file of user/action pairs; must restart API Server to change; not recommended |
| **RBAC** | Roles bound to users/groups/service accounts; standard |
| **Webhook** | Ask an external service |
| AlwaysAllow / AlwaysDeny | Testing |

Set with:

```
--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,Webhook
```

Modes are evaluated **in order**; the first that approves or denies decides. `Node` is checked first. If a mode says "no opinion", the next one is consulted. If none approve, the request is denied.

### Check the current mode

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep authorization-mode
ps -aux | grep kube-apiserver | grep authorization
```

### Testing

```bash
kubectl auth can-i create deployments
kubectl auth can-i delete nodes
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as dev-user
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as dev-user --namespace test
kubectl auth can-i --list
```

### Key takeaways

- Node,RBAC is the kubeadm default.
- `kubectl auth can-i` verifies permissions.
07-Security/17-RBAC:
### Introduction

Role-Based Access Control grants permissions to roles, then binds roles to subjects (users, groups, service accounts).

```
 Subject ◄── RoleBinding ──► Role ──► rules (apiGroups, resources, verbs)
```

### Role (namespaced)

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: developer
  namespace: default
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["list","get","create","update","delete"]
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps"]
  verbs: ["create"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  resourceNames: ["web"]          # restrict to specific objects
  verbs: ["get","update"]
```

Imperative:

```bash
kubectl create role developer --verb=list,get,create --resource=pods -n default
kubectl create role dev --verb=get --resource=pods --resource-name=blue,orange
```

### RoleBinding

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: devuser-developer-binding
  namespace: default
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: dev-user
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: developer
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

```bash
kubectl create rolebinding devuser-developer-binding --role=developer --user=dev-user
kubectl create rolebinding x --role=developer --group=devs
kubectl create rolebinding x --role=developer --serviceaccount=default:sa1
```

### Inspect

```bash
kubectl get roles
kubectl get rolebindings
kubectl describe role developer
kubectl describe rolebinding devuser-developer-binding
kubectl auth can-i create pods --as dev-user
```

### Key rules

- Roles and RoleBindings are **namespaced** and apply in their namespace only.
- Permissions are additive (no deny rules).
- `roleRef` is immutable after creation.
- A Pod can't get more rights than its service account.

### Troubleshooting

- "forbidden: User ... cannot list resource": missing role/binding, wrong namespace, wrong apiGroup, wrong verb.
- Mismatch between `kind: User` name and certificate CN.

### Key takeaways

- Role (what) + RoleBinding (who).

Q1. Which authorization modes does the API server use? ```bash kubectl describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane -n kube-system | grep authorization-mode ``` Typically `Node,RBAC`.
Q2. How do you list Roles and RoleBindings, and see what a Role allows? ```bash kubectl get roles,rolebindings -A kubectl describe role developer -n blue kubectl describe rolebinding dev-user-binding -n blue ```
Q3. Create a Role developer allowing a user to list, create and delete Pods in default, and bind it to dev-user. ```bash kubectl create role developer --verb=list,create,delete --resource=pods kubectl create rolebinding dev-user-binding --role=developer --user=dev-user ```

Q5. dev-user gets forbidden when getting a Pod. How do you fix it? Add the missing verb or resource to the Role (`kubectl edit role developer -n blue`). The Role must be in the same namespace as the Pod, and `resourceNames` must match if set.
07-Security/19-Cluster-Roles:
### Introduction

Some resources are cluster-scoped (nodes, PVs, namespaces), and sometimes you want rights across all namespaces. For those use ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding.

### Namespaced vs cluster-scoped

```bash
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false
```

### ClusterRole

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-admin
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["nodes"]
  verbs: ["get","watch","list","create","delete"]
```

### ClusterRoleBinding

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: node-admin-binding
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: cluster-admin-user
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: node-admin
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

```bash
kubectl create clusterrole node-admin --verb=get,list,watch --resource=nodes
kubectl create clusterrolebinding node-admin-binding --clusterrole=node-admin --user=michelle
```

### Cluster role with a RoleBinding

A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole to grant its permissions **inside one namespace** (reuse of common roles).

### Built-in cluster roles

`cluster-admin`, `admin`, `edit`, `view`, plus system roles (`system:node`, `system:kube-scheduler`...).

```bash
kubectl get clusterroles | wc -l
kubectl describe clusterrole view
```

### Key takeaways

- ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding = cluster-wide access.
07-Security/20-Practice-Test-Cluster-Rol:
Q1. Which ClusterRoles exist and how many are there? ```bash kubectl get clusterroles --no-headers | wc -l kubectl get clusterrolebindings --no-headers | wc -l ```
Q2. Create a ClusterRole that lets michelle list and get nodes, and bind it. ```bash kubectl create clusterrole node-admin --verb=get,list,watch --resource=nodes kubectl create clusterrolebinding michelle-binding --clusterrole=node-admin --user=michelle ```
Q3. Extend the same user to storage: allow list/get/create/delete on PersistentVolumes and PVCs. ```bash kubectl create clusterrole storage-admin --verb=list,get,create,delete --resource=persistentvolumes,storageclasses kubectl create clusterrolebinding michelle-storage --clusterrole=storage-admin --user=michelle ``` (PVCs are namespaced, so they need a Role/RoleBinding, or a ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding.)
Q4. Which resources are cluster-scoped? ```bash kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false ``` Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, Namespaces and ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped.
Q5. What is the difference between a RoleBinding and a ClusterRoleBinding that reference the same ClusterRole? A RoleBinding grants the ClusterRole's permissions only in its own namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding grants them cluster-wide.
07-Security/21-Service-Account:
### Introduction

A service account (SA) is an identity for applications running in Pods, used to authenticate to the API Server.

### Basics

```bash
kubectl create serviceaccount dashboard-sa
kubectl get sa
kubectl describe sa dashboard-sa
```

Each namespace has a `default` SA that Pods use unless they specify another.

### Tokens

Modern clusters (v1.24+):

- Pods get a **projected, time-limited token** automatically mounted at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/` (token, ca.crt, namespace).
- No long-lived Secret is created automatically.
- Create a token on demand:

```bash
kubectl create token dashboard-sa
kubectl create token dashboard-sa --duration=1h
```

- Legacy long-lived token Secret (if needed):

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: sa-token
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: dashboard-sa
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
```

### Use in a Pod

```yaml
spec:
  serviceAccountName: dashboard-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false     # optional: don't mount a token
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
```

The SA of an existing Pod can't be changed; Deployments allow it by editing the template.

### Authorising a service account

```bash
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding sa-binding --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=default:dashboard-sa
```

Subject form: `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>`.

### Using the token from outside

```bash
TOKEN=$(kubectl create token dashboard-sa)
curl -k https://<api>:6443/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

### Image pull secrets on a SA

```bash
kubectl patch sa default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'
```

### Key takeaways

- SAs are namespaced identities for Pods; bind roles to give permissions.
07-Security/22-Practice-Test-Service-Acc:
Q1. Create a ServiceAccount and a token. ```bash kubectl create serviceaccount dashboard-sa kubectl create token dashboard-sa ```
Q2. Make a Deployment use that ServiceAccount. Set `serviceAccountName: dashboard-sa` in the Pod template.
Q3. Why does the default token no longer appear as a Secret? Since v1.24 tokens are short-lived and requested via the TokenRequest API. Long-lived tokens need a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`.
Q4. How do you grant a ServiceAccount permissions? ```bash kubectl create rolebinding dash-rb --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=default:dashboard-sa ```
Q5. Which ServiceAccount does a Pod use if none is set? The `default` ServiceAccount of its namespace.
Q6. Stop a Pod mounting an API token. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` in the Pod or ServiceAccount spec.
07-Security/23-Image-Security:
### Introduction

Images come from registries. Private registries need credentials, which a Pod provides through an image pull secret.

### Image names

```
nginx                          = docker.io/library/nginx:latest
myrepo/app:1.2                 = docker.io/myrepo/app:1.2
gcr.io/project/app:v3          = registry gcr.io
private-registry.io/apps/web   = private registry
```

Avoid `:latest`; pin tags or, better, digests (`image@sha256:...`).

### Using a private registry

1. Create a Docker registry secret:

```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
  --docker-server=private-registry.io \
  --docker-username=registry-user \
  --docker-password=registry-password \
  --docker-email=registry-user@org.com
```

2. Reference it in the Pod:

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: private-registry.io/apps/internal-app
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: regcred
```

The secret must be in the **same namespace** as the Pod.

### Pull policy

`imagePullPolicy`: `Always`, `IfNotPresent`, `Never`. Default: `Always` for `:latest` or no tag, `IfNotPresent` otherwise.

### Troubleshooting

```bash
kubectl describe pod x      # ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff: "pull access denied" or "not found"
kubectl get secret regcred -o yaml
```

Typical causes: typo in name/tag, missing secret, wrong namespace, expired credentials.

### Key takeaways

- docker-registry secret + `imagePullSecrets`.
07-Security/24-Practice-Test-Image-Secur:
Q1. What image does a Pod use and from which registry? ```bash kubectl describe pod web | grep Image ``` An image name like `myregistry.io/app/web:1.0` has the registry first. Without a registry it defaults to Docker Hub (`docker.io`).
Q2. How do you create a Secret for a private registry? ```bash kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \ --docker-server=private-registry.io --docker-username=registry-user \ --docker-password=registry-password --docker-email=registry@org.com ```
Q3. How do you make a Pod pull from that registry? ```yaml spec: imagePullSecrets: - name: regcred containers: - name: app image: private-registry.io/apps/internal-app ```
Q4. A Pod is in ImagePullBackOff. How do you troubleshoot? ```bash kubectl describe pod # Events show the exact error ``` Common causes: typo in image or tag, private registry without `imagePullSecrets`, wrong credentials, registry unreachable.
Q5. Where does imagePullSecrets go if every Pod in a namespace needs it? Attach it to the ServiceAccount: `kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'`.
07-Security/25-Security-Context:
### Introduction

A security context sets privilege and access control for a Pod or container: which user runs the process, Linux capabilities, filesystem restrictions.

### Pod level vs container level

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-pod
spec:
  securityContext:              # applies to all containers
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsGroup: 3000
    fsGroup: 2000
  containers:
  - name: ubuntu
    image: ubuntu
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:            # overrides pod level for this container
      runAsUser: 1001
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        add: ["NET_ADMIN","SYS_TIME"]
        drop: ["ALL"]
```

**Capabilities** are only supported at the container level.

### Common fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup` | UID/GID of the process |
| `runAsNonRoot: true` | Refuse to start as root |
| `fsGroup` | Group owning mounted volumes |
| `privileged: true` | Nearly all host access (avoid) |
| `allowPrivilegeEscalation` | Block setuid gaining more privileges |
| `readOnlyRootFilesystem` | Immutable root filesystem |
| `capabilities` | Add/drop Linux capabilities |
| `seccompProfile`, `seLinuxOptions` | Kernel-level restrictions |

### Verify

```bash
kubectl exec web-pod -- whoami
kubectl exec web-pod -- id
kubectl exec web-pod -- ps aux
```

### Pod Security Standards

Namespace labels enforce `privileged`, `baseline`, or `restricted` profiles:

```bash
kubectl label ns dev pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
```

### Key takeaways

- Run as non-root, drop capabilities, read-only filesystem.
07-Security/26-Practice-Test-Security-Co:
Q1. What user does a container run as? ```bash kubectl exec -- whoami kubectl exec -- id ```
Q2. Run the Pod ubuntu-sleeper as user ID 1010. ```yaml spec: securityContext: runAsUser: 1010 containers: - name: ubuntu image: ubuntu command: ["sleep","4800"] ``` A Pod-level `securityContext` applies to all containers.
Q3. Add the Linux capabilities SYS_TIME and NET_ADMIN to a container. Capabilities are set per container, not on the Pod: ```yaml containers: - name: ubuntu image: ubuntu securityContext: capabilities: add: ["SYS_TIME","NET_ADMIN"] ```
Q4. A container-level and a Pod-level runAsUser disagree. Which wins? The container-level setting overrides the Pod-level one.
Q5. How do you stop a container running as root or escalating privileges? ```yaml securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true allowPrivilegeEscalation: false readOnlyRootFilesystem: true ```
07-Security/27-Network-Policies:
### Introduction

By default every Pod can talk to every other Pod. A NetworkPolicy restricts traffic to and from selected Pods, like a firewall. It needs a CNI that enforces it (Calico, Cilium, Weave; Flannel does **not**).

### Traffic model

```
 Ingress: traffic INTO selected Pods
 Egress:  traffic OUT of selected Pods
```

Rules are **allow lists**. As soon as a Pod is selected by a policy for a direction, all traffic in that direction is denied except what is allowed.

### Example: only the API Pod may reach the DB on 3306

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-policy
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: db
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: api-pod
      namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: prod
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 192.168.5.10/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3306
```

### AND vs OR in `from`

```yaml
# OR: two list items
from:
- podSelector: {...}
- namespaceSelector: {...}

# AND: one item with both
from:
- podSelector: {...}
  namespaceSelector: {...}
```

This indentation detail is a frequent exam trap.

### Selectors available

- `podSelector` (Pods in the policy's namespace).
- `namespaceSelector` (all Pods in matching namespaces).
- `ipBlock` (CIDR, with `except`).

### Egress example

```yaml
policyTypes: [Egress]
egress:
- to:
  - ipBlock: {cidr: 192.168.5.10/32}
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
```

Remember to allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) if you restrict egress.

### Default policies

```yaml
# deny all ingress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
# allow all ingress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  ingress:
  - {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
```

### Commands

```bash
kubectl get netpol
kubectl describe netpol db-policy
kubectl get pods --show-labels
```

### Testing

```bash
kubectl exec -it web -- nc -zv db 3306
kubectl exec -it web -- curl -m 3 http://db:3306
```

### Troubleshooting

- Policy seems ignored: CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy.
- Everything blocked: you selected the Pod with `policyTypes` but no allow rule; add rules.
- Check labels on Pods and namespaces (namespace labels needed for `namespaceSelector`; `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` is automatic).

### CKA exam tips

- Practise writing these from the docs (search "NetworkPolicy").
- Remember AND/OR and DNS for egress.

### Key takeaways

- Selected Pods become default-deny for the listed directions; add allow rules.
07-Security/28-Practice-Test-Network-Pol:
Q1. How do you list Network Policies and see which Pods one applies to? ```bash kubectl get netpol kubectl describe netpol payroll-policy ``` `podSelector` in the policy defines the target Pods.
Q2. Allow only the Pod labelled name=internal to reach payroll on port 8080. ```yaml apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: name: internal-policy spec: podSelector: matchLabels: name: payroll policyTypes: ["Ingress"] ingress: - from: - podSelector: matchLabels: name: internal ports: - port: 8080 ```
Q3. Allow egress from internal to mysql on 3306 and payroll on 8080. Add `Egress` to `policyTypes` and an `egress:` block with two `to:` entries and their `ports`. Remember DNS: allow UDP/TCP 53 egress too, or name lookups will fail.
Q4. What is the difference between a list of from entries and two selectors in one entry? Separate list items are ORed. Selectors in one item (for example `namespaceSelector` plus `podSelector`) are ANDed.
Q5. A policy exists but has no effect. Why? The CNI plugin must support Network Policies (Calico, Cilium, Weave do; Flannel alone does not). Also check the policy's namespace and labels.
07-Security/29-kubectx-and-kubens-comman:
### Introduction

`kubectx` and `kubens` are small helper tools to switch clusters (contexts) and namespaces quickly. They are not part of the exam environment, but the same operations are possible with `kubectl config`.

### kubectx

```bash
kubectx                  # list contexts
kubectx prod             # switch
kubectx -                # previous context
```

Equivalent: `kubectl config get-contexts` and `kubectl config use-context prod`.

### kubens

```bash
kubens                   # list namespaces
kubens kube-system       # switch default namespace
kubens -                 # previous
```

Equivalent: `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=kube-system`.

### Install

```bash
sudo git clone https://github.com/ahmetb/kubectx /opt/kubectx
sudo ln -s /opt/kubectx/kubectx /usr/local/bin/kubectx
sudo ln -s /opt/kubectx/kubens /usr/local/bin/kubens
```

### Key takeaways

- Convenience tools; know the plain `kubectl config` commands for the exam.
08-Storage/02-Introduction-to-Docker-Sto:
### Introduction

Before Kubernetes storage, understand how containers handle data. Containers are ephemeral; when they are removed their data goes with them unless it is stored outside.

### Two kinds of Docker storage

1. **Storage drivers / layered filesystem** - how image and container layers are stored.
2. **Volume drivers** - how persistent data is stored.

### Layered architecture

An image is a stack of read-only layers (one per Dockerfile instruction). A running container adds a thin writable layer on top.

```
 ┌───────────────────────┐
 │ container layer (R/W) │  deleted with the container
 ├───────────────────────┤
 │ image layer 4 (RO)    │
 │ image layer 3 (RO)    │
 │ image layer 2 (RO)    │
 │ image layer 1 (RO)    │
 └───────────────────────┘
```

Layers are cached and shared among images, which saves space and speeds builds.

**Copy-on-write**: modifying a file from an image layer copies it up into the writable layer first.

### Key takeaways

- Data in the writable layer is lost when the container is removed; use volumes.
08-Storage/03-Storage-in-Docker:
### Introduction

How Docker keeps data beyond the life of a container.

### Volumes and bind mounts

```bash
docker volume create data_volume           # /var/lib/docker/volumes/data_volume
docker run -v data_volume:/var/lib/mysql mysql      # volume mount
docker run -v /data/mysql:/var/lib/mysql mysql      # bind mount (host path)
docker run --mount type=bind,source=/data/mysql,target=/var/lib/mysql mysql
```

| Type | Location | Managed by |
|---|---|---|
| Volume mount | `/var/lib/docker/volumes/...` | Docker |
| Bind mount | Any host path | You |
| tmpfs | Memory | Host (non-persistent) |

If you use a volume name that doesn't exist, Docker creates it.

### Storage drivers

Docker chooses one based on the OS: `overlay2` (common), `aufs`, `zfs`, `btrfs`, `device mapper`. They implement the layered filesystem.

### Key takeaways

- Use volumes for persistence; drivers handle layers.
08-Storage/04-Volume-Driver-Plugins-in-D:
### Introduction

Volumes are handled by **volume driver plugins**. The default is `local`. Others can provide remote storage: Azure File Storage, GlusterFS, Portworx, NetApp, REX-Ray (AWS EBS, S3, Google Persistent Disk) and more.

```bash
docker run -it --name mysql --volume-driver rexray/ebs --mount src=ebs-vol,target=/var/lib/mysql mysql
```

This creates a volume on a cloud disk, persisting even if the host disappears.

### Key takeaways

- Plugins let containers use external storage backends.
- This is the precursor of the Kubernetes Container Storage Interface.

### Why this matters for Kubernetes

Docker's volume plugins hid storage details behind a driver. Kubernetes took the same idea further: instead of each runtime having plugins, the **CSI** standard lets any vendor ship a driver that works in any orchestrator. When you see `provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com` in a StorageClass, that's the descendant of a Docker volume driver.

```
Docker:       container ─► volume driver (rexray/ebs) ─► cloud disk
Kubernetes:   Pod ─► PVC ─► StorageClass ─► CSI driver ─► cloud disk
```
08-Storage/05-Container.Storage-Interfac:
### Introduction

Kubernetes originally had storage code built in for each backend. The **Container Storage Interface (CSI)** is a standard so any storage vendor can write a plugin without modifying Kubernetes.

### The three interfaces

| Interface | Standardises |
|---|---|
| CRI | Container runtimes (Docker, containerd, CRI-O) |
| CNI | Networking plugins |
| CSI | Storage plugins |

### What CSI defines

Remote procedure calls the orchestrator uses, such as `CreateVolume`, `DeleteVolume`, `ControllerPublishVolume`. The storage vendor implements them in a **CSI driver**, usually deployed as a controller Deployment plus a node DaemonSet.

```
 Kubernetes ──CSI RPC──► driver (Portworx, EBS, Ceph, NetApp...) ──► storage backend
```

### In practice

```bash
kubectl get csidrivers
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep csi
```

A StorageClass names the driver in `provisioner:`.

### Key takeaways

- CSI is the standard storage plugin API; it works with any container orchestrator.
08-Storage/06-Volumes:
### Introduction

A Pod's container filesystem is ephemeral. A **volume** attaches storage to a Pod that lives as long as the Pod (or longer, for external volumes) and is shared among its containers.

### Basic example

```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo $(date) >> /opt/number.out; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /opt
      name: data-volume
  volumes:
  - name: data-volume
    hostPath:
      path: /data
      type: Directory
```

`volumes` defines the storage; `volumeMounts` places it in a container.

### Common volume types

| Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `emptyDir` | Empty directory created when the Pod starts, deleted with the Pod; shared between containers; can be in memory (`medium: Memory`) |
| `hostPath` | Directory from the node's filesystem; data stays on that node; avoid on multi-node |
| `configMap`, `secret`, `downwardAPI`, `projected` | Inject configuration |
| `persistentVolumeClaim` | Use a PersistentVolume (next lessons) |
| `nfs`, `awsElasticBlockStore`, `csi`, ... | External storage |

### Why hostPath is limited

On a multi-node cluster, Pods may land on different nodes and see different data. Use real network or cloud storage via PVs.

### emptyDir sharing

```yaml
volumes:
- name: cache
  emptyDir: {}
```

Two containers in the Pod can mount it to exchange files.

### Key takeaways

- `volumes` + `volumeMounts`; volume types decide the backend.
08-Storage/07-Persistent-Volumes:
### Introduction

Defining storage in every Pod is not scalable. A **PersistentVolume (PV)** is a cluster-wide pool of storage created by an admin. Users claim from it using PVCs.

```
 Admin ─► PV (10Gi)       User ─► PVC (5Gi) ─► binds ─► Pod uses PVC
```

### PV definition

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-vol1
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: manual
  hostPath:
    path: /tmp/data         # lab only
```

Production: replace `hostPath` with `nfs`, `csi`, cloud disk, etc.

### Access modes

| Mode | Short | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| ReadWriteOnce | RWO | One node read/write |
| ReadOnlyMany | ROX | Many nodes read-only |
| ReadWriteMany | RWX | Many nodes read/write |
| ReadWriteOncePod | RWOP | One Pod only |

### Reclaim policy

What happens to the PV after its claim is deleted:

| Policy | Result |
|---|---|
| `Retain` (default for manual PVs) | PV stays, `Released`, data kept, needs manual cleanup |
| `Delete` | PV and backing storage are deleted (default for dynamic) |
| `Recycle` | Deprecated |

### Phases

`Available` → `Bound` → `Released` → (`Failed`).

```bash
kubectl get pv
kubectl describe pv pv-vol1
```

PVs are cluster-scoped (no namespace).

### Key takeaways

- PV = the storage resource; capacity, access mode, reclaim policy.
08-Storage/08-Persistent-Volume-Claims:
### Introduction

A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** is a user's request for storage. Kubernetes binds each PVC to a suitable PV.

### PVC

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: myclaim
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Mi
  storageClassName: manual
```

### Binding rules

The controller finds a PV where:

- `capacity` >= requested size
- access modes include the requested one
- `storageClassName` matches
- selectors/labels match if specified (`selector.matchLabels`)

Binding is **one to one**. A 1Gi PV bound by a 500Mi claim wastes the rest. If no PV matches, the PVC stays `Pending` (unless dynamic provisioning applies).

```bash
kubectl get pvc
kubectl get pv
kubectl describe pvc myclaim
```

### Deleting a PVC

Depends on the PV's reclaim policy (Retain/Delete). PVCs in use by a Pod are protected (`kubernetes.io/pvc-protection`) until the Pod is gone.

### Troubleshooting a Pending PVC

- Size too large for any PV.
- Access mode mismatch.
- `storageClassName` mismatch (even empty vs set).
- No PV available, and no default StorageClass.

### Key takeaways

- PVC requests, PV supplies; match on size, access mode, class.
08-Storage/09-Using-PVC-in-PODs:
### Introduction

Pods consume claims by referencing them in `volumes`.

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: mypod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: "/var/www/html"
      name: mypd
  volumes:
  - name: mypd
    persistentVolumeClaim:
      claimName: myclaim
```

The same works for ReplicaSets and Deployments (in the Pod template). The PVC must be in the same namespace as the Pod.

### Check

```bash
kubectl get pod mypod
kubectl describe pod mypod       # Volumes section, events
kubectl exec mypod -- df -h /var/www/html
kubectl exec mypod -- sh -c 'echo hi > /var/www/html/x'
```

### Troubleshooting

- Pod `Pending`: unbound PVC or no schedulable node for the volume.
- `ContainerCreating`: mount failure; see events.
- Data gone: you used `emptyDir` or the PV was `Delete`/hostPath on another node.

### Key takeaways

- Pod → PVC → PV → storage.

08-Storage/12-Storage-Class:
### Introduction

Manual PV creation does not scale. A **StorageClass (SC)** enables **dynamic provisioning**: when a PVC requests the class, the provisioner creates the storage and PV automatically.

```
 PVC (storageClassName: fast) ─► StorageClass fast ─► provisioner ─► disk + PV created ─► bound
```

### Definition

```yaml
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: google-storage
provisioner: kubernetes.io/gce-pd
parameters:
  type: pd-ssd
  replication-type: none
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
```

### Fields

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provisioner` | Driver that creates volumes (CSI driver name) |
| `parameters` | Provisioner-specific settings (type, IOPS) |
| `reclaimPolicy` | `Delete` (default) or `Retain` for created PVs |
| `volumeBindingMode` | `Immediate` or `WaitForFirstConsumer` (wait for a Pod to be scheduled) |
| `allowVolumeExpansion` | Allow resizing PVCs |

### PVC using the class

```yaml
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: google-storage
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Mi
```

### Default class

```bash
kubectl get sc                           # (default) marker
kubectl patch sc standard -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
```

A PVC without `storageClassName` uses the default class; `storageClassName: ""` means no class (static binding only).

### Local storage

`provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner` plus `WaitForFirstConsumer` for local PVs, where you create PVs yourself.

### Key takeaways

- StorageClass = automatic PV creation with chosen parameters.

09-Networking/01-Networking-Introduction:
### Introduction

Kubernetes networking builds on ordinary Linux networking. This section first covers prerequisites (switching, routing, DNS, namespaces, Docker networking, CNI), then Kubernetes cluster networking, Pod networking, Services, DNS and Ingress.

### Roadmap

```
 prerequisites:  switching/routing ─ DNS ─ network namespaces ─ Docker networking ─ CNI
 cluster:        node ports, Pod network (CNI), Service network (kube-proxy)
 discovery:      CoreDNS
 exposure:       Services, Ingress
```

### Key takeaways

- If you know Linux networking basics, skip the prerequisites; otherwise they explain everything later.

### What you must be able to do by the end of this section

1. Explain how Pods get IP addresses and reach each other across nodes (CNI).
2. Explain what a ClusterIP is and how kube-proxy implements it.
3. Resolve Services by DNS and fix CoreDNS problems.
4. Expose applications with NodePort, Ingress or Gateway API.
5. Write NetworkPolicies (covered in Security).
6. Troubleshoot connectivity layer by layer.

### Connectivity debug ladder

```
 Pod → Pod IP        (CNI)
 Pod → Service IP    (kube-proxy, endpoints)
 Pod → Service name  (CoreDNS)
 outside → app       (NodePort / Ingress / Gateway)
```

Test from the bottom up and stop at the first layer that fails.
09-Networking/02-Pre-requisite-Switching:
### Introduction

How machines talk on a network.

### Switching

A **switch** connects hosts on one network (e.g. 192.168.1.0/24). Each host has an interface (`eth0`).

```bash
ip link                         # list interfaces
ip addr add 192.168.1.10/24 dev eth0
ip addr show
```

Hosts on the same network communicate through the switch without a router.

### Routing

A **router** connects different networks (192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24). It has an IP on each. Hosts need a route to tell them where to send traffic for other networks.

```bash
ip route                        # or route
ip route add 192.168.2.0/24 via 192.168.1.1
ip route add default via 192.168.1.1
```

### Gateway

The gateway is the router address a host uses to leave its network. The **default gateway** (`0.0.0.0/0`) handles anything with no specific route.

### Linux as a router

By default Linux does not forward packets between interfaces.

```bash
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward        # 0 = off
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
# permanent: /etc/sysctl.conf  net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
```

### Diagnostics

```bash
ping 192.168.2.5
traceroute 192.168.2.5
ip route get 192.168.2.5
```

### Key takeaways

- Switch = same network; router = between networks; route entries + gateways.
- IP forwarding must be enabled for a Linux router (and Kubernetes nodes need it).
09-Networking/03-Pre-requisite-DNS:
### Introduction

DNS maps names to IP addresses.

### Local name resolution

`/etc/hosts` maps names to IPs on a single machine:

```
192.168.1.11   db
```

For many hosts, use a DNS server. Point hosts at it in `/etc/resolv.conf`:

```
nameserver 192.168.1.100
search mycompany.com prod.mycompany.com
```

Order of lookup is in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (`hosts: files dns`: files first, then DNS).

### Domain hierarchy

```
 root (.) ─► com ─► google ─► www
 www.google.com  = host www in domain google.com
```

`search` domains let you type `web` and resolve `web.mycompany.com`.

### Record types

| Type | Maps |
|---|---|
| A | name → IPv4 |
| AAAA | name → IPv6 |
| CNAME | name → another name (alias) |
| MX, TXT, SRV, PTR | mail, text, service location, reverse |

### Tools

```bash
ping web
nslookup www.google.com        # ignores /etc/hosts
dig www.google.com
host web
```

### Key takeaways

- Files, then DNS; `resolv.conf` sets the server and search domains.
09-Networking/04-Pre-requisite-CoreDNS:
### Introduction

CoreDNS is a flexible DNS server written in Go, and it's the default DNS in Kubernetes.

### Running it

```bash
wget https://github.com/coredns/coredns/releases/...
./coredns
```

It listens on port 53 and is configured with a **Corefile** made of plugins:

```
.:53 {
    errors
    health
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
        pods insecure
        fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
}
```

The `hosts` plugin can serve entries from a file, and `kubernetes` serves cluster records.

### Key takeaways

- CoreDNS = pluggable DNS configured by the Corefile.

### Worked example: a tiny local DNS server

```
# Corefile
. {
    hosts /tmp/hosts {
        fallthrough
    }
    forward . 8.8.8.8
    log
}
```

```
# /tmp/hosts
192.168.1.10   web.example.test
```

```bash
./coredns -conf Corefile
dig @127.0.0.1 web.example.test
```

Plugins run in the order defined by CoreDNS (not the file order), `fallthrough` passes unanswered queries on, and `forward` sends them upstream. In Kubernetes the same Corefile lives in the `coredns` ConfigMap.
09-Networking/05-Pre-requisite-Network-N:
### Introduction

Linux **network namespaces** isolate network stacks: each has its own interfaces, routes and ARP table. Containers use them for isolation.

### Create and use

```bash
ip netns add red
ip netns add blue
ip netns list
ip netns exec red ip link          # run a command inside
ip -n red link                     # shorter
```

The namespace sees none of the host's interfaces.

### Connect two namespaces with a virtual cable

```bash
ip link add veth-red type veth peer name veth-blue
ip link set veth-red netns red
ip link set veth-blue netns blue
ip -n red addr add 192.168.15.1/24 dev veth-red
ip -n blue addr add 192.168.15.2/24 dev veth-blue
ip -n red link set veth-red up
ip -n blue link set veth-blue up
ip netns exec red ping 192.168.15.2
```

### Many namespaces: a virtual bridge

For more than two, create a bridge switch on the host:

```bash
ip link add v-net-0 type bridge
ip link set dev v-net-0 up
ip link add veth-red type veth peer name veth-red-br
ip link set veth-red netns red
ip link set veth-red-br master v-net-0
ip -n red addr add 192.168.15.1/24 dev veth-red
ip -n red link set veth-red up
ip link set veth-red-br up
```

Give the bridge an IP so the host can reach namespaces: `ip addr add 192.168.15.5/24 dev v-net-0`.

### Reaching the outside

```bash
ip netns exec blue ip route add default via 192.168.15.5
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.15.0/24 -j MASQUERADE
```

### Reaching inwards (port forwarding)

```bash
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.15.2:80
```

### Key takeaways

- Namespace = isolated network stack; veth pairs + bridge + NAT connect it. This is what container runtimes automate.
09-Networking/06-Pre-requisite-Docker-Ne:
### Introduction

How Docker uses namespaces, bridges and NAT to network containers. Kubernetes uses similar ideas.

### Network modes

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `none` | No network |
| `host` | Shares the host's network (no isolation; port conflicts) |
| `bridge` (default) | Private internal network `172.17.0.0/16` via `docker0` bridge |

```bash
docker run --network none nginx
docker run --network host nginx
docker network ls
ip addr show docker0
```

### How bridge mode works

For each container Docker creates a namespace and a veth pair attached to the bridge. Containers on the bridge reach each other by IP.

### Port mapping

Containers are not reachable from outside by default. Publish ports:

```bash
docker run -p 8080:80 nginx
```

Docker adds an iptables NAT rule:

```
iptables -t nat -A DOCKER -j DNAT --dport 8080 --to-destination 172.17.0.3:80
```

```bash
iptables -nvL -t nat
```

### Key takeaways

- Bridge + veth + iptables NAT = Docker networking.
- Kubernetes needs a different model (every Pod reachable without NAT), supplied by CNI plugins.
09-Networking/07-Pre-requisite-CNI:
### Introduction

Every container runtime repeated the same networking steps. The **Container Network Interface (CNI)** defines a standard so runtimes and network plugins interoperate.

### The standard

For the runtime (kubelet/containerd): create a namespace, identify the network, invoke the plugin on **add** and **delete**, and handle the JSON config.

For the plugin: support `ADD`, `DEL`, `CHECK` commands, take container ID and namespace, assign IPs, set up routes, return results.

```
 runtime ──► plugin ADD(container id, netns, config) ──► IP, routes assigned
```

### Plugins

bridge, vlan, ipvlan, macvlan, host-device (built-in); Weave, Flannel, Calico, Cilium, Cisco ACI, VMware NSX and others (third-party).

**Docker does not implement CNI**; it uses its own CNM (container network model). That's why Kubernetes with Docker created its networking manually with `--network=none` and the CNI plugin.

### Key takeaways

- CNI = plugin standard for container networking; Kubernetes uses it.
09-Networking/08-Cluster-Networking:
### Introduction

What networking a Kubernetes cluster needs between its nodes and components.

### Node requirements

- Each node has at least one interface on the node network with an IP, a unique hostname and a unique MAC address.
- Required open ports:

| Port | Component | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 6443 | kube-apiserver | control plane |
| 10250 | kubelet API | all nodes |
| 10259 | kube-scheduler | control plane |
| 10257 | kube-controller-manager | control plane |
| 2379 | etcd client | control plane |
| 2380 | etcd peer | control plane |
| 30000–32767 | NodePort services | workers |

Firewalls and security groups must allow these. (In clusters with multiple control planes, ETCD ports are open between them.)

### Commands to explore

```bash
ip link ; ip addr
ip addr show eth0
ip route
netstat -nplt             # listening ports (or ss -tlnp)
netstat -anp | grep etcd
arp node01
```

### Notable details

- The API server listens on 6443, ETCD on 2379 (clients) and 2380 (peers). Because there are more client connections to 2379, etcd on multiple control planes needs both.
- The kubelet's port 10250 and the control plane component ports are used by health checks and metrics.

### Key takeaways

- Know the port table.

Q2. Find the interface used for the cluster network and its MAC. ```bash ip link ip addr show eth0 ```

Q4. How do you find a Pod's IP and node? ```bash kubectl get pods -o wide ```
Q5. Which network ranges does a cluster use? Node network, Pod CIDR, and Service CIDR (`--service-cluster-ip-range`).
Q6. Show the routing table of a node. ```bash ip route ```
09-Networking/10-Pod-Networking:
### Introduction

Kubernetes expects a flat Pod network. The model:

- Every Pod gets its own IP.
- Pods on the same node can communicate.
- Pods on different nodes can communicate **without NAT**.

Kubernetes doesn't implement this; a CNI plugin does.

### Manual illustration

Each node gets a Pod subnet (e.g. 10.244.1.0/24, 10.244.2.0/24). On each node:

```
 node1                                node2
 ┌─────────────────┐                 ┌─────────────────┐
 │ bridge v-net-0  │                 │ bridge v-net-0  │
 │ 10.244.1.1/24   │                 │ 10.244.2.1/24   │
 │ pod 10.244.1.2  │                 │ pod 10.244.2.2  │
 └────────┬────────┘                 └────────┬────────┘
          └────────── node network ───────────┘
 routes: node1: 10.244.2.0/24 via node2 IP ; node2: 10.244.1.0/24 via node1 IP
```

### What the CNI script does

When a Pod is created, the runtime calls the plugin which:

1. Creates a veth pair.
2. Attaches one end to the Pod namespace and the other to the bridge.
3. Assigns an IP (from the node's Pod CIDR) and adds routes.
4. Brings the interfaces up.

On delete it removes them.

### Routes between nodes

Implemented as host routes, an overlay (VXLAN), or BGP (Calico). Plugins do this automatically.

### Key takeaways

- Flat Pod network, no NAT, with per-node Pod CIDRs.
09-Networking/11-CNI-in-Kubernetes:
### Introduction

How Kubernetes finds and calls the CNI plugin.

### Who invokes CNI

The container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) creates the Pod sandbox and calls the CNI plugin. The kubelet provides the configuration via the runtime settings.

### Where it's configured

```
/opt/cni/bin/               plugin executables (bridge, host-local, flannel, ...)
/etc/cni/net.d/             configuration files (first file alphabetically is used)
```

```bash
ls /opt/cni/bin
ls /etc/cni/net.d
cat /etc/cni/net.d/10-flannel.conflist
```

### A config

```json
{
  "cniVersion": "0.3.1",
  "name": "mynet",
  "type": "bridge",
  "bridge": "cni0",
  "isGateway": true,
  "ipMasq": true,
  "ipam": {
    "type": "host-local",
    "subnet": "10.244.0.0/16",
    "routes": [{ "dst": "0.0.0.0/0" }]
  }
}
```

The `type` is the plugin, `ipam` decides IP allocation, `isGateway` gives the bridge an IP, `ipMasq` enables NAT for outside access.

### Check which plugin runs

```bash
ps aux | grep kubelet           # container-runtime-endpoint
kubectl -n kube-system get pods # weave-net / calico / flannel
```

### Troubleshooting

- Nodes `NotReady` with "network plugin not ready: cni config uninitialized": no CNI installed.
- Pods stuck in `ContainerCreating` with errors about CNI: plugin Pods not running, or config missing.

### Key takeaways

- Binaries in `/opt/cni/bin`, config in `/etc/cni/net.d`.
09-Networking/12-CNI-weave:
### Introduction

Weave Net is a CNI plugin that creates an overlay network. A Weave agent runs on each node, they learn about each other and encapsulate traffic between nodes.

```
 node1: weave peer ◄═══ encapsulated traffic ═══► weave peer :node2
        pod A ──► weave bridge                      weave bridge ──► pod B
```

### Deploying

Weave runs as a DaemonSet, one Pod per node:

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://reweave.azurewebsites.net/k8s/v1.29/net.yaml
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep weave
kubectl logs -n kube-system weave-net-xxxxx -c weave
```

### Inspect

```bash
ip link | grep weave            # weave bridge
ip addr show weave
kubectl -n kube-system get ds weave-net
```

Default Pod network range `10.32.0.0/12`.

### Other CNI choices

| Plugin | Notes |
|---|---|
| Flannel | Simple overlay; **no NetworkPolicy** |
| Calico | BGP/routing; NetworkPolicy; popular |
| Cilium | eBPF; NetworkPolicy, observability |
| Weave | Overlay; NetworkPolicy support |

### Key takeaways

- Weave = DaemonSet overlay; check its Pods and bridge interface.
09-Networking/13-Practice-Test-CNI-weave:
Q1. Which CNI plugin is installed and where is its config? ```bash ls /etc/cni/net.d/ ls /opt/cni/bin ```
Q2. Pods are stuck ContainerCreating. Why? Often no CNI is installed. `kubectl describe pod` shows "network plugin is not ready".
Q3. Which binary does the kubelet run to set up Pod networking? The one named in the CNI config, such as `weave-net` or `flannel`, found in `/opt/cni/bin`.
Q4. What does CNI stand for and what does it do? Container Network Interface: a standard for plugins that assign Pod IPs and set up connectivity.
Q5. Which CNI plugins support Network Policies? Calico, Cilium and Weave do; Flannel does not.
Q6. Show the CNI config in use. ```bash cat /etc/cni/net.d/*.conflist ```
09-Networking/14-Practice-Test-Deploy-Ne:
Q1. Deploy Weave Net. ```bash kubectl apply -f https://reweave.azurewebsites.net/k8s/v1.29/net.yaml ``` (Use the manifest URL from the lab or Weave docs.)
Q2. How do you confirm it works? ```bash kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep weave ``` Then check that previously stuck Pods become `Running`.
Q3. Pods get IPs from the wrong range. How do you change it? Set `IPALLOC_RANGE` in the weave container env of the DaemonSet.
Q4. Why do nodes show NotReady before a CNI is installed? The kubelet reports the network plugin as not ready until a CNI config exists.
Q5. Does every Pod need a unique IP? Yes. Kubernetes requires every Pod to reach every other Pod without NAT.
Q6. Where do you set the Pod CIDR for kubeadm? `kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=`, and it must match the CNI's range.
09-Networking/15-ipam-weave:
### Introduction

IP Address Management (IPAM) decides how Pods receive unique IP addresses. The CNI plugin delegates to an IPAM plugin.

### Options

- **host-local**: each node has its own subnet and a local file tracks allocations. Simple; the cluster must carve out per-node ranges.
- **Weave's IPAM**: allocates from a shared range, split dynamically among peers. Default range `10.32.0.0/12` divided across nodes.
- **Calico IPAM**, cloud-specific IPAMs.

### Config

```json
"ipam": {
  "type": "host-local",
  "subnet": "10.244.1.0/24"
}
```

### Check

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'
kubectl get pods -A -o wide     # Pod IPs
```

### Key takeaways

- IPAM ensures unique Pod IPs; the node CIDR (`--pod-network-cidr`, `--cluster-cidr`) matters.
09-Networking/16-Practice-Test-Networkin:
Q1. How many Weave agents run and where? One per node (DaemonSet): `kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep weave`.
Q2. What is the Pod network range and the bridge name? ```bash ip addr show weave kubectl logs -n kube-system weave-net-xxxx -c weave | grep ipalloc-range ```
Q3. What is the default gateway of a Pod? ```bash kubectl exec -it -- ip route ``` It points to the bridge IP on the Pod's node.
Q4. Which command shows Weave's status? ```bash kubectl exec -n kube-system weave-net-xxxxx -c weave -- /home/weave/weave --local status ```
Q5. How does traffic cross nodes with Weave? Weave agents form a mesh and encapsulate Pod traffic between nodes.
Q6. How do you find which node's agent a Pod uses? ```bash kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep weave ```
09-Networking/17-Service-Networking:
### Introduction

How Service IPs work. Services are cluster-wide virtual objects: no process, no interface. Kube-proxy on every node turns them into forwarding rules.

### Ranges

```
Pod network       10.244.0.0/16     (CNI)
Service network   10.96.0.0/12      (--service-cluster-ip-range on the API server)
```

The two ranges must not overlap with each other or the node network.

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system describe pod kube-apiserver-controlplane | grep service-cluster-ip-range
```

### Creation flow

```
 Service created ─► kube-proxy on each node watches the API
                  ─► adds rules: ClusterIP:port → Pod IP:port
```

### Types as rules

- **ClusterIP**: rule on each node for internal use.
- **NodePort**: also listens on a port on each node (30000–32767).

### See the rules

```bash
iptables -t nat -L -n | grep db-service
iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES | head
```

Rule comments show `default/db-service`. Log: `/var/log/kube-proxy.log` or Pod logs.

### Mode options

kube-proxy `--proxy-mode`: `iptables` (default), `ipvs`, `nftables`.

### Key takeaways

- Service IPs are virtual and implemented as NAT rules by kube-proxy.

09-Networking/19-DNS-in-kubernetes:
### Introduction

Kubernetes runs an internal DNS server so Pods find Services by name.

### Service records

For a Service `web-service` in namespace `apps`:

```
web-service                              (same namespace)
web-service.apps
web-service.apps.svc
web-service.apps.svc.cluster.local       (fully qualified)
```

Root domain `cluster.local`, then `svc`, then namespace.

### Pod records

Not created by default; if enabled, Pods get names such as `10-244-2-5.apps.pod.cluster.local` (dots replaced by dashes).

### How Pods use it

The kubelet writes `/etc/resolv.conf` in each Pod:

```
nameserver 10.96.0.10          # the kube-dns Service IP
search apps.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5
```

The search list makes short names work. `ndots:5` means names with fewer than five dots try the search domains first.

### Test

```bash
kubectl run test --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup web-service
kubectl exec -it pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
kubectl run test --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup web-service.apps.svc.cluster.local
```

### Key takeaways

- `service.namespace.svc.cluster.local`; resolv.conf search domains make short names work.
09-Networking/20-CoreDNS-in-Kubernetes:
### Introduction

CoreDNS is the cluster DNS. It runs as a Deployment (two replicas) in `kube-system` behind the `kube-dns` Service.

### Components

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get deploy coredns
kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns
kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml
```

### Corefile ConfigMap

```
.:53 {
    errors
    health { lameduck 5s }
    ready
    kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
       pods insecure
       fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
       ttl 30
    }
    prometheus :9153
    forward . /etc/resolv.conf
    cache 30
    loop
    reload
    loadbalance
}
```

- `kubernetes` plugin handles `cluster.local`.
- `forward . /etc/resolv.conf` sends everything else to the node's resolvers.
- Edit the ConfigMap and CoreDNS reloads (`reload` plugin) or restart the Pods: `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy coredns`.

### How Pods find CoreDNS

The kubelet sets `--cluster-dns=10.96.0.10` and `--cluster-domain=cluster.local` in `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`:

```bash
grep -A2 clusterDNS /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
```

### Troubleshooting DNS

```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
kubectl get endpoints kube-dns -n kube-system
kubectl run t --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default
```

Common causes: CoreDNS Pods down, wrong Corefile, loop plugin detecting a loop with `/etc/resolv.conf` pointing to itself, NetworkPolicy blocking port 53, wrong `clusterDNS`.

### Key takeaways

- CoreDNS Deployment + `kube-dns` Service + Corefile ConfigMap.

09-Networking/22-Ingress:
### Introduction

NodePort and LoadBalancer expose one Service each. **Ingress** is a layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS) router that exposes many Services through one entry point using URL paths or hostnames, and also handles TLS.

```
 Internet ─► [Ingress controller (NodePort/LB)] ─► rules ─► Service A (/wear)
                                                       └──► Service B (/watch)
```

### Two parts

1. **Ingress controller** - the software that does the work (NGINX, Traefik, HAProxy, Istio, Contour). **Not installed by default.**
2. **Ingress resources** - rules the controller reads.

### Deploy a controller (NGINX example)

Needs a Deployment, a Service to expose it (NodePort/LB), a ConfigMap, a ServiceAccount with the right RBAC, and an `IngressClass`.

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.11.0/deploy/static/provider/baremetal/deploy.yaml
kubectl -n ingress-nginx get all
kubectl get ingressclass
```

### Ingress resource

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: ingress-wear-watch
  namespace: app-space
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /wear
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: wear-service
            port:
              number: 80
      - path: /watch
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: video-service
            port:
              number: 80
```

By host:

```yaml
rules:
- host: wear.my-online-store.com
  http:
    paths:
    - path: /
      pathType: Prefix
      backend: {service: {name: wear-service, port: {number: 80}}}
```

### Imperative

```bash
kubectl create ingress ingress-test --rule="wear.my-online-store.com/wear*=wear-service:80"
kubectl get ingress
kubectl describe ingress ingress-wear-watch
```

### Path types

`Exact`, `Prefix`, `ImplementationSpecific`.

### Default backend

Requests matching no rule go to the default backend (404 page unless configured).

### TLS

```yaml
spec:
  tls:
  - hosts: [shop.example.com]
    secretName: shop-tls
```

### Troubleshooting

- 404 from the controller: path, host or service name/port mismatch; check `describe ingress` for `<error: endpoints ... not found>`.
- 503: Service has no ready endpoints.
- Ingress ignores rules: wrong `ingressClassName`.
- Backend service must be in the same namespace as the Ingress.

### CKA exam tips

- Know `kubectl create ingress` and the YAML shape; `pathType` is required.

### Key takeaways

- Controller + resource; L7 routing by path/host.
09-Networking/23-Ingress-Annotations-and:
### Introduction

Annotations configure controller-specific behaviour. The most common is **rewrite-target**, which changes the URL path passed to the backend.

### The problem

A user visits `/watch`; the Ingress routes to the video Service, which serves content at `/`. Without rewriting, the backend receives `/watch` and returns 404.

### Rewrite

```yaml
metadata:
  name: rewrite
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /pay
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: pay-service
            port: {number: 8282}
```

`rewrite-target: /` makes `http://host/pay` reach the backend as `/`.

### With a capture group

```yaml
annotations:
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /$2
spec:
  rules:
  - http:
      paths:
      - path: /something(/|$)(.*)
        pathType: ImplementationSpecific
        backend: ...
```

`/something/foo` → `/foo`.

### Other useful annotations (NGINX)

| Annotation | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect` | Force HTTPS |
| `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size` | Upload limit |
| `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/whitelist-source-range` | Allowed IPs |

### Key takeaways

- Annotations are controller specific; rewrite-target fixes path mismatches.

10-Design-and-Install-Kubernetes-Cluster:
### Introduction

Before building a cluster, decide what it is for, how big it must be, and what it will run. The design drives the infrastructure choice, node sizes and high-availability needs.

### Purpose

| Purpose | Suggested setup |
|---|---|
| Education / learning | Minikube, kind, k3s, or a single-node kubeadm cluster on a laptop or cloud VM |
| Development / testing | Multi-node cluster, one control plane, several workers; managed service is fine |
| Production hosting | HA control plane (3 nodes), multiple workers, monitoring, backups |

### Production guidance

- Up to **5,000 nodes**, **150,000 Pods**, **300,000 containers**, **100 Pods per node** are the documented upper limits.
- HA: multiple control plane nodes, ideally across failure zones.
- Workers: size to the workload (CPU, memory, disk type, network).
- Use SSD-backed disks for ETCD; consider running ETCD on dedicated nodes for big clusters.

### Workload considerations

| Workload | Needs |
|---|---|
| CPU/memory heavy | Large instances, dedicated node pools, taints |
| Disk intensive | SSD, local storage, fast StorageClasses |
| GPU | GPU nodes with device plugin, taints/tolerations |
| Many small Pods | Many medium nodes |

### Node basics

- 64-bit Linux, a supported container runtime (containerd).
- Control plane nodes do not run workloads (taints).
- Master nodes can host ETCD (stacked) or use external ETCD.

### Key takeaways

- Define purpose, scale, and workload type first; the answers decide the rest.

### Introduction

Where and how to run Kubernetes: laptop, on-premise, or cloud; self-managed or managed.

### Local / learning

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| Minikube | Single-node VM or container |
| kind | Clusters in Docker containers, great for CI |
| k3s | Lightweight distribution |
| kubeadm | Bootstraps real clusters on Linux machines |
| Docker Desktop | Single-node built-in |

### Self-hosted (turnkey vs custom)

- **Turnkey**: you provision VMs, a tool configures the cluster (kubeadm, Kubespray, kops, OpenShift, Rancher).
- **Hosted / managed**: the provider runs the control plane (GKE, EKS, AKS, DigitalOcean). You manage workloads and sometimes workers.

| Choice | You manage | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Self-managed on VMs | Everything | Full control | Operational work |
| Managed | Workloads + workers | Less ops, easy upgrades | Less control, cost |

### Choosing

Consider: team skills, cost, compliance, scale, vendor lock-in, upgrade and support needs.

### Key takeaways

- Learn with kubeadm; run production on managed services unless you need control.

### Introduction

A single control plane node is a single point of failure. In an HA cluster you run several control plane nodes behind a load balancer.

```
            kubectl / kubelets
                   │
            ┌──────▼──────┐
            │ Load balancer│  (HAProxy / nginx / cloud LB)  :6443
            └──┬────┬───┬──┘
               ▼    ▼   ▼
             CP1   CP2  CP3
```

### Which components are active

| Component | HA behaviour |
|---|---|
| kube-apiserver | **Active/active**; all instances serve requests |
| kube-scheduler | **Active/passive** via leader election |
| kube-controller-manager | **Active/passive** via leader election |
| ETCD | Raft cluster (leader + followers) |

Leader election uses `--leader-elect=true`, a Lease object in `kube-system`:

```bash
kubectl -n kube-system get lease
```

### Load balancer

Point `kubectl`, kubelets and all components at the LB address, not at a single API server. With kubeadm:

```bash
kubeadm init --control-plane-endpoint "lb.example.com:6443" --upload-certs
kubeadm join lb.example.com:6443 --control-plane --certificate-key <key> --token ...
```

The API server certificate must include the LB DNS name/IP in its SANs.

### Quorum

With ETCD on the control plane nodes you need an odd count: 3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2.

### Key takeaways

- API servers active/active behind an LB; scheduler and controller manager elect a leader.

### Introduction

ETCD must also be highly available. This lesson covers topology and quorum for ETCD in HA clusters.

### Topologies

| Topology | Description | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| **Stacked** | ETCD on the same nodes as the control plane | Simple, fewer machines; losing a node loses both |
| **External** | ETCD on dedicated nodes | More resilience, more machines |

### Quorum and fault tolerance

`quorum = floor(N/2) + 1`.

| N | Quorum | Tolerates |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0 |
| 3 | 2 | 1 |
| 5 | 3 | 2 |
| 7 | 4 | 3 |

Use odd numbers; 3 or 5 is typical. An even number gives no extra tolerance (4 tolerates 1, like 3). In a network split, the side with the majority continues.

### Setting up

Each member is started with:

```
--name etcd-1
--initial-advertise-peer-urls https://10.0.0.1:2380
--listen-peer-urls https://10.0.0.1:2380
--listen-client-urls https://10.0.0.1:2379,https://127.0.0.1:2379
--advertise-client-urls https://10.0.0.1:2379
--initial-cluster-token etcd-cluster-1
--initial-cluster etcd-1=https://10.0.0.1:2380,etcd-2=https://10.0.0.2:2380,etcd-3=https://10.0.0.3:2380
--initial-cluster-state new
```

The API server lists all members: `--etcd-servers=https://10.0.0.1:2379,https://10.0.0.2:2379,https://10.0.0.3:2379`.

### Operations

```bash
etcdctl member list -w table
etcdctl endpoint status --cluster -w table
etcdctl endpoint health --cluster
```

### Key takeaways

- 3 or 5 members; losing quorum stops writes.
11-Install-Kubernetes-the-kubeadm-way/01:
### Introduction

`kubeadm` is the official tool for bootstrapping a Kubernetes cluster on existing machines. It automates certificates, static Pod manifests, and join tokens. It does not provision machines or install a network plugin.

### The process

```
 1. Provision machines (VMs)
 2. Install a container runtime (containerd) + kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl on ALL nodes
 3. kubeadm init   on the control plane node
 4. Install a CNI (Pod network) add-on
 5. kubeadm join   on each worker node
```

### Prerequisites

- 2 CPU, 2 GB RAM minimum per machine for control plane (more for production).
- Unique hostname, MAC address and product_uuid.
- Required ports open (6443, 10250, 2379-2380, 30000-32767).
- Swap disabled.
- Kernel modules `overlay`, `br_netfilter` and sysctl settings for bridged traffic.

### Key takeaways

- kubeadm sets up Kubernetes components; you provide machines, runtime and CNI.

11-Install-Kubernetes-the-kubeadm-way/04:
### Introduction

The full sequence of building a cluster with kubeadm.

### 1. On every node: prepare

```bash
swapoff -a
cat <<EOF | tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
overlay
br_netfilter
EOF
modprobe overlay ; modprobe br_netfilter
cat <<EOF | tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables  = 1
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward                 = 1
EOF
sysctl --system
```

### 2. Install runtime and Kubernetes packages

```bash
apt-get install -y containerd
mkdir -p /etc/containerd ; containerd config default > /etc/containerd/config.toml
# set SystemdCgroup = true
systemctl restart containerd

apt-get install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl gpg
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.31/deb/Release.key | gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.31/deb/ /' > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list
apt-get update
apt-get install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl
apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl
systemctl enable --now kubelet
```

### 3. Initialise the control plane

```bash
kubeadm init --apiserver-advertise-address=192.168.56.2 \
             --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
```

Note the `kubeadm join` command printed at the end. Configure kubectl:

```bash
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
cp -i /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
```

### 4. Install a CNI

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/releases/latest/download/kube-flannel.yml
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
```

The Pod CIDR must match `--pod-network-cidr`.

### 5. Join workers

```bash
kubeadm join 192.168.56.2:6443 --token abcdef.0123456789abcdef --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:...
```

Regenerate the command if the token expired (24h):

```bash
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
```

### 6. Verify

```bash
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -A
```

### Troubleshooting

- Nodes `NotReady`: no CNI yet, or kubelet issues.
- `kubeadm init` pre-flight errors: swap on, ports in use, runtime missing.
- cgroup driver mismatch between kubelet and containerd: set `SystemdCgroup = true`.
- `kubeadm reset` to start over.

### Key takeaways

- Prepare nodes, init, CNI, join, verify.

12-Troubleshooting/02-Application-Failur:
### Introduction

Troubleshooting an application: follow the request path and check each hop.

### Typical architecture

```
 user ─► web Service ─► web Pods ─► db Service ─► db Pods
```

### Method

1. Start from the user's symptom (cannot reach the app).
2. Walk each layer: Service, Pods, dependencies, configuration.
3. Use logs and events.

### Checks, in order

```bash
# Service
kubectl get svc
kubectl describe svc web-service           # selector, port, targetPort, Endpoints
kubectl get endpoints web-service          # empty means no matching ready Pods
kubectl get pods --show-labels             # compare labels with selector

# Pods
kubectl get pods
kubectl describe pod web
kubectl logs web
kubectl logs web --previous                # after a restart

# Dependencies (DB)
kubectl get svc mysql-service ; kubectl describe svc mysql-service
kubectl get pods ; kubectl logs mysql
```

### Common causes

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| Service has no endpoints | Selector/labels mismatch, Pods not Ready |
| Connection refused | Wrong `targetPort`, app not listening |
| `CrashLoopBackOff` | Bad command, missing config, DB unreachable |
| App can't reach DB | DB service name/port, env variables, DB credentials, namespace |
| Intermittent errors | Probes, resource limits, node issues |

### Test connectivity

```bash
kubectl exec web -- curl -s db-service:3306
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- nslookup db-service
```

### Key takeaways

- Check Service → Endpoints → Pod → logs → dependencies.

### Introduction

A worked method to solve application failure labs.

### Steps and answers

1. `kubectl get all -n <ns>` for an overview.
2. Frontend not reachable: `kubectl describe svc webapp-service` → check selector and NodePort; compare with Pod labels. Fix a typo in the selector (`name: webapp-mysql` vs `name: webapp`).
3. Backend unreachable: `kubectl describe svc mysql-service` → targetPort; the Service name must match the DB host in the web app's env (`DB_Host`).
4. Credentials: `DB_User` / `DB_Password` in the web Deployment must match MySQL's `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`.
5. NodePort: confirm the expected `nodePort` in the Service spec.
6. Fix with `kubectl edit`, wait for the rollout, test again in the browser or with `curl`.

### Pattern to remember

```bash
kubectl edit svc web-service            # selector/ports
kubectl edit deploy webapp-mysql        # env/ports
kubectl rollout status deploy/webapp-mysql
```

### Tip

Change one thing at a time and re-test so you know which fix worked.
12-Troubleshooting/04-Control-Plane-Fail:
### Introduction

When the cluster itself misbehaves, check the control plane components and their configuration.

### Quick checks

```bash
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
```

If `kubectl` itself fails, the API server is down: use the node.

### kubeadm cluster (components are static Pods)

```bash
kubectl logs kube-apiserver-controlplane -n kube-system
crictl ps -a | grep kube
crictl logs <container-id>
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests
journalctl -u kubelet
```

### Service-based cluster

```bash
systemctl status kube-apiserver
journalctl -u kube-apiserver
service kube-controller-manager status
```

### Common failures and where to look

| Symptom | Component | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| `kubectl` connection refused | kube-apiserver | wrong flag/cert path in manifest, ETCD unreachable |
| Pods stay Pending, no events | kube-scheduler | scheduler down, bad kubeconfig path |
| Deployments don't create Pods | kube-controller-manager | down, bad config |
| Replica counts wrong | controller manager | |
| API timeouts | etcd | wrong data dir / certs |
| Node NotReady | kubelet | service down, config |

### Manifest mistakes to look for

- Typo in a flag or filename (`--kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conff`).
- Wrong path in `volumes.hostPath` versus the `volumeMounts` (certificates).
- Wrong image name or tag.
- Wrong port or command (`kube-schedulerr`).

### Fix procedure

1. Read the logs.
2. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/<component>.yaml`.
3. Wait for the kubelet to restart the Pod (may take a minute).
4. Verify.

Always keep a backup copy before editing.

### Key takeaways

- Identify the failing component, read its logs, fix the manifest.

12-Troubleshooting/06-Solution-Control-P:
### Introduction

Solutions for typical control plane failures.

### Examples

1. **Pods stuck Pending**: scheduler Pod in `CrashLoopBackOff`. Logs say the config path is wrong. Edit the manifest to the real path and let the kubelet recreate the Pod.
2. **Scaling does nothing**: `kube-controller-manager` crashing; logs reveal missing certificate file; the hostPath in the manifest points to a non-existent directory. Correct the `path:` under `volumes` to `/etc/kubernetes/pki`.
3. **Both fixed**: verify `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` all `Running`.

### Checklist

- Compare each flag path with files in the actual directory (`ls /etc/kubernetes/pki`).
- Check that `volumeMounts.mountPath` and `volumes.hostPath.path` pair up.
- Wait about a minute after saving.

### Order of checks

1. `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` (which Pod is not Running?).
2. `kubectl logs` / `crictl logs` (what exactly is wrong?).
3. Compare the manifest against reality: `ls` every path it names.
4. Edit, save, wait, verify with a functional test (scale a Deployment, create a Pod).

A functional test matters: a Pod can be `Running` while still misconfigured.
12-Troubleshooting/07-Worker-Node-Failur:
### Introduction

Worker problems usually show up as a node in `NotReady` or `Unknown`.

### Diagnose

```bash
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node worker-1
```

Look at **Conditions**: `Ready`, `MemoryPressure`, `DiskPressure`, `PIDPressure`, `NetworkUnavailable`. `Unknown` means the kubelet stopped reporting (crash, network, node down).

On the node:

```bash
top ; df -h ; free -m
systemctl status kubelet
journalctl -u kubelet
systemctl status containerd
ss -tlnp | grep 10250
```

### Certificates

```bash
openssl x509 -in /var/lib/kubelet/worker-1.crt -text -noout      # validity and issuer
```

An expired or wrong kubelet certificate prevents registration.

### Typical causes

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| kubelet stopped | `systemctl start kubelet`, `enable` |
| Wrong CA / kubeconfig path | edit `/etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf` or `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` |
| Wrong API server address/port | fix `server:` in `kubelet.conf` (6443) |
| Runtime stopped | `systemctl restart containerd` |
| Disk full | clean up |
| Swap on | disable |

### Key takeaways

- `describe node` for conditions, `journalctl -u kubelet` for reasons.

### Introduction

Hands-on practice of JSONPath queries against kubectl output. JSONPath is a query language to extract fields from JSON; kubectl uses it with `-o jsonpath`.

### Method

1. Look at the structure first: `kubectl get pods -o json | less` (or `-o yaml`).
2. Build the path from the root: `.items[0].spec.containers[0].image`.
3. Use `[*]` for all elements, `[?(@.key=="value")]` for filters.
4. Format with `range` loops and `{"\n"}` / `{"\t"}`.

### Examples

```bash
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.nodeInfo.osImage}'
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.podIP}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get pv -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.capacity.storage}'
```

### Tips

- Save the output to files when asked: `> /opt/outputs/nodes.txt`.
- `kubectl explain` finds field names.
- Quote the expression in single quotes.

### Practice set

```bash
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].image}'
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}'
kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.nodeName}{"\n"}{end}'
kubectl get deploy -A -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u
```

Debug trick: an empty result usually means a wrong key, a missing `.items` (list vs single object) or `[0]` vs `[*]` mix-up.
13-Other-Topics/02-Pre-Requisites-JSON-P:
### Introduction

JSONPath basics before using it with kubectl.

### JSON refresher

```json
{
  "car": { "color": "blue", "price": 20000 },
  "bus": { "color": "red", "price": "100000" },
  "wheels": [ { "model": "KDJ39", "location": "rear-right" }, { "model": "TRE45", "location": "front-left" } ]
}
```

### JSONPath syntax

| Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$` | Root |
| `$.car.color` | Child by key |
| `$.wheels[0].model` | Array index |
| `$.wheels[*].model` | All elements |
| `$[?(@.price>1000)]` | Filter |
| `$..model` | Recursive search |
| `$[0:3]` | Slice |
| `$[-1:]` | Last element |

In kubectl the root `$` is implicit and the expression goes in braces.

### Lists in JSONPath

kubectl output of multiple objects is a `List` with `.items`. A query on one resource has no `.items`.

### Formatting

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}{"\n"}{.items[*].status.capacity.cpu}{"\n"}'
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.capacity.cpu}{"\n"}{end}'
```

### Custom columns and sorting

```bash
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NODE:.metadata.name,CPU:.status.capacity.cpu
kubectl get nodes --sort-by=.metadata.name
```

### Key takeaways

- Learn `[*]`, filters and `range`.
